summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change telecommunications laws to reduce industry red tape, strengthen consumer protections, and improve the co-regulatory framework.

It would require the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman scheme to meet standards set by the Minister after consulting the TIO and the Australian Communications and Media Authority, and mandate periodic independent public reviews of the scheme.

The bill would also allow industry codes to be varied instead of wholly replaced, require code developers to publish draft codes and public submissions online, and clarify the meaning of 'cause' in the Do Not Call Register Act for telemarketing calls made by third parties.
changes: Require the TIO scheme to comply with Minister-determined standards.
Require periodic public reviews of the TIO scheme by an independent body.
Allow industry codes to be varied rather than wholly replaced.
Extend the reimbursement scheme for developing consumer-related codes to cover variations.
Require code developers to publish draft codes and public submissions on their websites.
Clarify the meaning of 'cause' in the Do Not Call Register Act for telemarketing calls made by third parties.
summary.affected: The telecommunications industry, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, the Australian Communications and Media Authority, and the Department of Communications.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: Moved the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, arguing that it would reduce regulatory burdens, strengthen enforcement of the Do Not Call Register Act 2006, allow telecommunications codes to be updated more efficiently, and require periodic independent review of the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman scheme.

speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, which Labor introduced in government, noted a Senate committee inquiry received six submissions and reported in late June, and warned the Do Not Call Register should not be targeted by the government's planned early-2014 regulation repeal day.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013 in her first speech on proposed legislation, noting approximately nine million telephone numbers are listed on the Do Not Call Register, and described her elderly mother being repeatedly targeted by telemarketers despite being registered.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, but criticised the government for removing rollout timeline information from the NBN Co website for Wollongong-area suburbs, and presented a national petition against the coalition's broadband policy that had gathered 270,640 signatures by 26 November.

speeches.speaker: Bernie Ripoll
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, which Labor wrote in government, credited former Speaker Anna Burke for championing the Do Not Call and Do Not Knock initiatives, and criticised ongoing problems with slow and inconsistent broadband access under the existing copper network.

speeches.speaker: Ed Husic
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, noting that of Australia's 22 million people, nine million have registered on the Do Not Call Register, representing nearly two-thirds of fixed line telephone subscribers.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Backed the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013 for letting industry codes be varied without full replacement and requiring changes to be published online, and cited analysis showing the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman registered 215,000 complaints in 2009-10, almost 25 times the United Kingdom's rate.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Welcomed the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013 for ending the current two to three year process required to remake industry codes for minor changes, citing Optus chief executive Kevin Russell's example of a $3,000 bill run up by a 16-year-old and almost one million complaints to the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, welcoming provisions closing a loophole that let companies contract out telemarketing calls to avoid the Do Not Call Register, and urged the government not to let red tape reduction erode consumer protections.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, noting that nine million landlines are now registered on the Do Not Call Register, credited former Speaker Anna Burke for championing the register, and welcomed changes requiring third parties who make telemarketing calls to be held responsible.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013, describing constituents in Bedford unable to get help from the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman over unreliable internet, and a new subdivision left without any telecommunications connection because no Telstra pit existed in the street.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: Summed up the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Consumer Protection) Bill 2013 as Minister for Communications, describing new powers for the Australian Communications and Media Authority against telemarketers using overseas third parties, and noted the bill builds on the Telecommunications Act 1997, introduced by the Howard government sixteen years ago.
